title: Mass psychogenic illness
description: Spread of illness without organic cause
wiki_lead: Mass psychogenic illness (MPI), also called mass sociogenic illness, mass psychogenic disorder, epidemic hysteria or mass hysteria, involves the spread of illness symptoms through a population where there is no infectious agent responsible for contagion. It is the rapid spread of illness signs and symptoms affecting members of a cohesive group, originating from a nervous system disturbance involving excitation, loss, or alteration of function, whereby physical complaints that are exhibited unconsciously have no corresponding organic causes that are known.
grok_lead: Mass psychogenic illness (MPI) is the rapid spread of illness signs and symptoms affecting members of a cohesive group, originating from a nervous system disturbance and lacking identifiable organic pathology despite extensive investigation. Symptoms typically include headache, dizziness, nausea, weakness, and hyperventilation, manifesting suddenly and propagating through social contagion mechanisms such as suggestion, anxiety modeling, and shared beliefs rather than direct causal agents like toxins or pathogens. Episodes often arise in high-stress, enclosed settings like schools or workplaces, disproportionately involving adolescents and females, with empirical data indicating psychosocial triggersâsuch as perceived threats from odors or rumorsâamplifying underlying vulnerabilities like dissociation proneness. Historically documented from medieval phenomena like dancing manias to contemporary outbreaks, MPI resolves swiftly upon environmental separation and authoritative reassurance, affirming its basis in collective psychological dynamics over physical etiology. Diagnostic controversies persist, as initial organic attributions delay recognition, fueled by institutional reluctance to invoke psychogenic explanations amid biases favoring measurable pathologies, yet peer-reviewed analyses consistently validate MPI through exclusion of alternatives and observation of symptom clustering independent of exposure.
